title: Supported Employment
shortDescription: Job coaching that helps autistic adults find and keep a competitive job in the community.
description:
Supported employment helps autistic adults find and keep competitive jobs in the community, with a job coach providing on-site training, employer communication, and ongoing support for as long as it is needed. In Florida it is most often funded through the Agency for Persons with Disabilities iBudget waiver or through Vocational Rehabilitation, and providers are enrolled with the state rather than billed through health insurance. The goal is integrated employment at regular wages, not a separate workplace for people with disabilities. Availability varies considerably by region, and waiting lists are common.

How this gets paid for in Florida is worth understanding before you start calling providers. The waiver route runs through the iBudget program administered by the Agency for Persons with Disabilities (APD), and a person generally has to be enrolled in the waiver before a provider can bill for this service. There are more eligible applicants than funded slots, so APD maintains a pre-enrollment list, and APD reports more than 23,000 people waiting for waiver services. Placement is not first-come, first-served: under section 393.065(5), Florida Statutes, APD sorts applicants into priority categories and uses a Pre-enrollment Prioritization Tool to decide who receives an enrollment offer as funding becomes available.

Supported employment is the one service in this group with a real alternative route, which is worth knowing if you are not on the waiver. Vocational Rehabilitation is a separate state program run by the Department of Education, with its own application and no waiver requirement. APD also runs an Employment Enhancement Project that funds supported employment for some people who are still on the pre-enrollment list. If the person you are supporting is not on the APD list yet, the place to start is an application to your regional APD office — and there is no reason to wait on that list before contacting Vocational Rehabilitation as well.
benefits: A job coach provides on-site training at the actual worksite
Support continues for as long as it is needed, not just during placement
The coach can handle communication with the employer and coworkers
Competitive, integrated employment at regular wages
Help with job searching, applications, and interviews
Two funding routes in Florida — the APD waiver and Vocational Rehabilitation
whoCanBenefit: Autistic adults who want to work in the community
Students and young adults transitioning out of school services
People who can do the work but struggle with the hiring process
Those who have lost jobs due to workplace communication or sensory barriers
Anyone moving from adult day training toward paid employment
